promptText: How should a startup founder working solo organize their team's work?
rawText:
Organizing "team" work as a solo founder sounds like a paradox, but it is actually the secret to staying sane and building a scalable business. 

When you are solo, you are not one person doing one job; **you are one person occupying five executive roles.** If you don't organize your work by *function* rather than by *person*, you will suffer from severe context-switching fatigue and lose track of critical business needs.

Here is a practical, step-by-step framework to organize your startup’s work as a solo founder.

---

### 1. Adopt the "Multi-Hat" Framework
Define the core departments of your business and explicitly assign yourself to each role. Typically, a solo startup consists of four major roles:
*   **CEO (Vision & Strategy):** Fundraising, high-level planning, legal, financial management.
*   **CPO/CTO (Product & Engineering):** Building, designing, fixing bugs, technical architecture.
*   **CMO (Marketing & Growth):** Content creation, sales calls, SEO, customer acquisition.
*   **COO/CSO (Ops & Customer Support):** Responding to support tickets, invoicing, admin work.

**The Rule:** *Never wear two hats at the exact same time.* When you are writing code (CTO), turn off your marketing notifications (CMO). When doing deep strategic planning (CEO), close your support inbox (COO).

---

### 2. Implement a Theme-Based Weekly Rhythm
Context switching kills productivity. Instead of doing a little bit of everything every day, group your functions into specific days or blocks of time.

*   **Monday (CEO & Ops):** Metrics review, weekly planning, financial admin, deep strategic work.
*   **Tuesday – Thursday (Product/Maker Days):** Uninterrupted build time. Coding, product design, or core service delivery. Zero sales calls if possible.
*   **Friday (Marketing & Growth):** Writing content, running ads, outbound sales, networking, customer outreach.
*   **Daily "Admin Sandwich" (30 mins morning / 30 mins evening):** Customer support and email triage. Do not touch email during your mid-day execution blocks.

---

### 3. Use an "Agile for One" Project System
Run your solo company on 1-week or 2-week "Sprints." 

*   **Tooling:** Use a simple visual board (Notion, Trello, Linear, or ClickUp). 
*   **Structure:** Create four columns: 
    1.  *Backlog* (Every idea you have—keep it out of your head).
    2.  *This Week's Sprint* (Only tasks committed for the current week).
    3.  *In Progress* (Maximum of 1 or 2 items at a time).
    4.  *Done*.
*   **The Weekly Planning Ritual:** Every Sunday evening or Monday morning, look at your Backlog and move *only* what is humanly possible into "This Week's Sprint." Once the sprint starts, do not add new tasks unless it is a business-critical emergency.

---

### 4. Leverage "Ghost Teammates" (AI & Automation)
Treat software and AI tools as your virtual junior employees. Assign them specific "jobs":

*   **AI as your Copywriter/Researcher:** Use ChatGPT or Claude to draft social media posts, generate outreach emails, or summarize research.
*   **Automation as your Operations Lead:** Use Zapier or Make to connect your tools (e.g., auto-saving invoices to Google Drive, sending leads from a Webflow form straight to your CRM).
*   **Scheduling Tools as your EA:** Use Calendly or SavvyCal to eliminate back-and-forth emails for meetings.

---

### 5. Document Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) Early
You won’t be solo forever. Organize your work *today* as if you are training your replacement *tomorrow*.

*   **The "Rule of Two":** If you have to perform a operational task more than twice (e.g., deploying code, onboarding a new client, publishing a blog post), record your screen using **Loom** while doing it.
*   Save that video in a centralized "Company Handbook" (in Notion or Google Drive). 
*   **Why this works:** It creates a systemized process for you to follow now (reducing mental tax) and makes hiring your first freelancer or employee effortless later.

---

### 6. Conduct a "Solo Retrospective" Every Friday
At the end of the week, spend 15 minutes asking yourself three executive questions:
1.  *What got done this week that actually moved the revenue/product needle?*
2.  *Where did I waste time or get distracted?*
3.  *What task did I hate doing that I should automate, eliminate, or delegate next?*

### Summary Checklist for the Solo Founder
* [ ] **One Central Tool:** Pick *one* tool (like Notion or Linear) as your Single Source of Truth.
* [ ] **Time Blocking:** Schedule dedicated, uninterrupted blocks for "Maker" work and "Manager" work.
* [ ] **Asynchronous First:** Avoid real-time meetings with clients/advisors when an email or Loom video will do.
* [ ] **Protect Energy, Not Just Time:** Do high-brainpower tasks (coding, writing) when your energy is highest, and low-brainpower tasks (admin, inbox zero) when you are tired.
